p.src: Now the king, ministers, and people of the Kingdom of Bhiksu escorted the four pilgrims more than twenty li beyond the city, still reluctant to part with them. Tripitaka finally persuaded them to let him descend from the carriage; he mounted his horse, bade them farewell, and set off, while those seeing him off watched until every trace of the party had vanished before turning back. The four traveled on for a long while; the last of winter passed and spring drew to its close, and everywhere they saw wildflowers, mountain trees, and luxuriant scenery. Ahead of them another lofty, precipitous mountain came into view. Alarmed, Tripitaka asked, “Disciple, is there a road through that high mountain ahead or not? You must be careful.” Pilgrim laughed. “Master, that is hardly the talk of a seasoned traveler. You sound more like some pampered young lord who has seen no farther than the sky from the bottom of a well. As the old saying goes, ‘A mountain does not block the road; the road makes its own way through the mountain.’ Why ask whether there is a road?” Tripitaka said, “Though it is true that mountains do not block the road, I fear monsters may lurk among the crags and demons emerge from the depths of the dense woods.” Bajie said, “Set your mind at ease, set your mind at ease. We are drawing near to the Land of Ultimate Bliss now; it cannot be far away. I guarantee we shall have peace and no trouble.”

p.src: While master and disciples were speaking, they unknowingly reached the foot of the mountain. Pilgrim took out his gold-banded staff, climbed onto a rocky ledge, and called, “Master, here is a path that winds around the mountain. It is wonderfully easy going. Come quickly, come quickly!” The elder had no choice but to put aside his fears and urge his horse forward. Friar Sand said, “Second Brother, carry the luggage on your shoulder for a while.” Bajie duly took the load and shouldered it, while Friar Sand gathered up the reins. With their old master sitting securely in the carved saddle, they followed Pilgrim and all made for the broad road along the cliff. This was the mountain they saw:

p.src: Pilgrim said, “Master, you are forever thinking of home. You do not behave at all like one who has left the world. Set your mind at ease and keep going; do not fret so much. The ancients said, ‘Whoever seeks prosperity in life must labor with a will to die.’” Tripitaka said, “What you say is reasonable, disciple, but I still do not know where the road to the Western Heaven may be.” Bajie said, “Master, perhaps our Buddha, the Tathagata, cannot bear to part with those Tripitaka scriptures. Knowing we are coming to fetch them, he may have moved them elsewhere; otherwise, why do we never manage to reach them?” Friar Sand said, “Do not talk nonsense. Just keep following Elder Brother. If we persevere and endure, the day will surely come when we arrive.”

p.src: The Great Sage Sun was utterly unafraid. Wielding his iron staff, he went ahead and cleared open the main path, leading Tang Sanzang straight into the depths of the forest. They traveled along at their ease for half a day, yet still saw no way out of the forest. Tang Sanzang called, “Disciples, ever since we set out westward, we have crossed countless rugged mountains and forests. Fortunately, this place is serene and refined, and the road has been peaceful. The wondrous flowers and strange plants in this forest are truly pleasing to the heart. I should like to sit here awhile: first, to rest the horse; and second, because I am hungry. Go somewhere and beg some vegetarian food for me.” Pilgrim said, “Please dismount, Master. Old Sun will go and beg for food.” The elder duly dismounted, and Bajie tied the horse to a tree. Friar Sand set down the luggage, took out the alms bowl, and handed it to Pilgrim. Pilgrim said, “Sit here in peace, Master, and do not be alarmed. I shall return as soon as I have gone.” Tripitaka sat upright beneath the shade of the pines, while Bajie and Friar Sand went off to look for flowers and fruit and amuse themselves.

p.src: Now the Great Sage turned a somersault and rose into midair. Halting his cloud, he looked back and saw auspicious clouds drifting through the pine forest and blessed vapors gathering thickly. Suddenly he cried out, “Wonderful! Wonderful!” Why, you may ask, did he cry out in praise? He was in fact praising Tang Sanzang, saying that his master was the reincarnation of Elder Golden Cicada, a good man cultivated through ten lifetimes, and that this was why such auspicious signs hovered above his head. “As for old Sun, five hundred years ago, when I caused havoc in Heaven, I roamed the ends of the seas and wandered freely to the farthest corners of the earth; I gathered hordes of spirits and proclaimed myself the Great Sage Equaling Heaven; I subdued dragons and tigers and erased my name from the register of death. On my head I wore a triple-crested golden crown; on my body, golden armor; in my hand I held the gold-banded staff; and beneath my feet I wore cloud-treading shoes. Under my command were forty-seven thousand monsters, all of whom addressed me as Grandfather Great Sage. I was truly a figure of consequence. Now I have escaped the calamities decreed by Heaven, humbled myself, and become your disciple. Since auspicious clouds and blessed vapors surely hover above Master’s head, his return to the Eastern Land will certainly bring some good outcome, and old Sun too will surely attain the true fruit.”

p.src: While he was thus praising and reflecting to himself, he suddenly saw a stream of black vapor south of the forest, bubbling thickly upward. Pilgrim was greatly startled. “There must be something evil in that black vapor. Neither Bajie nor Friar Sand knows how to emit black vapor like that.” The Great Sage remained in midair, scrutinizing it but unable to determine what it was.

p.src: Now Tripitaka sat in the forest, clarifying his mind and perceiving his true nature as he recited the Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Great Wisdom, when suddenly he heard a faint, sobbing cry: “Save me!” Tripitaka was greatly startled and said, “Merciful heavens! Who could be calling out in such a deep forest? Perhaps someone has been frightened and felled by wolves, tigers, or leopards. Let me go and see.” The elder rose and made his way past thousand-year-old cypresses and ten-thousand-year-old pines, clinging to creepers and climbing vines until he drew near to look. There he saw a woman bound to a great tree, the upper half of her body tied to the trunk with creepers and the lower half buried in the earth. The elder stopped and asked her, “Good lady, what has happened to leave you bound here?” Ah! The creature was plainly a demon, but the elder, with his mortal eyes and fleshly frame, could not recognize it. When the creature saw him approach and question her, tears gushed from her eyes like springs. See how tears streamed down her peach-blossom cheeks, from a face lovely enough to sink fish and bring down geese; grief filled her star-bright eyes, and her beauty could shame the moon and make flowers hide. The elder dared not draw closer, but asked again, “Good lady, what offense have you truly committed? Tell this poor monk, so that I may know how to save you.” With artful words, flowery speech, and feigned emotion, the demon hurriedly replied, “Master, my family lives in the Kingdom of the Poor Woman, more than two hundred li from here. My parents are both alive, exceedingly charitable, and have spent their whole lives living peaceably with kin and kindly toward friends. When the Qingming Festival came, they invited all our relatives and every member of the clan to sweep the ancestral graves, and our whole procession of sedan chairs and horses traveled into the desolate countryside. At the graves we laid out the offerings, but just as we burned the paper horses, gongs and drums sounded and a band of brigands rushed out, brandishing blades and staves and charging us with battle cries, so that our souls nearly fled our bodies. My parents and relatives who could seize a horse or sedan chair each escaped with their lives; but I was only a young girl. Unable to run, I collapsed in terror and was carried off into the mountains by the brigands. Their chief wanted me for his consort, the second chief wanted me for his wife, the third and fourth were both enamored of my beauty, and all seventy or eighty of them quarreled over me. None would yield to the others, so they bound me here in the forest and scattered to their separate camps. Five days and five nights have now passed; my life is nearly spent, and before long I shall die. I know not in what former age my ancestors accumulated the virtue that has brought a venerable master like you here today. I beg you to show boundless compassion and save my life. Even beneath the Nine Springs, I shall never forget your kindness.” When she had finished, her tears fell like rain.

p.src: Tripitaka was truly tenderhearted; unable to restrain himself, he too shed tears and called out in a choking voice, “Disciples!” Bajie and Sha Monk were searching for flowers and fruit in the forest when they suddenly heard their master calling so mournfully. The fool said, “Brother Sha, has Master found a relative here?” Sha Monk laughed and said, “Second Brother, what nonsense! We have traveled all this time without meeting even one decent person. Where could a relative have come from?” Bajie said, “If it is not a relative, why is Master weeping with someone over there? Let us go and see.” Sha Monk indeed returned to their former place, led the horse and shouldered the luggage, then came before the master and asked, “Master, what is the matter?” The Tang Monk pointed at the tree and cried, “Bajie, untie that good lady and save her life.” Without pausing to distinguish right from wrong, the fool went straight over and set to work.

p.src: Meanwhile, the Great Sage, still in midair, again saw that the black vapor had grown dense and completely covered the auspicious radiance. He cried, “This is bad, very bad! The black vapor has shrouded the auspicious light. Can some demon be harming my master? Begging for food is a small matter; I had better go and see my master first.” He turned his cloud around, descended into the forest, and saw Bajie fumbling about as he untied the ropes. Pilgrim stepped forward, seized him by the ear, and with a thump hurled him to the ground. The fool looked up and saw who it was. Scrambling to his feet, he said, “Master told me to save someone. Why do you rely on your strength to throw me down like that?” Pilgrim laughed and said, “Brother, do not untie her. She is a demon making a commotion to deceive us.” Tripitaka shouted, “You impudent monkey, you are talking nonsense again! How can you take such a woman for a demon?” Pilgrim replied, “Master, you do not understand. Old Monkey has practiced this very trade before. These are the tricks used by those who want to eat human flesh. How could you recognize them?” Bajie thrust out his lips and said, “Master, do not believe this Protector of the Horses when he tries to fool you. This woman belongs to a family from these parts. We have come from the distant Eastern Land, have no quarrel with her, and are not her kin. On what grounds does he call her a demon? He sends us away to continue on ahead, then turns a somersault, works his magic, and comes back to have his pleasure with her. He means to steal a march on us!” Pilgrim shouted, “You clumsy oaf, stop your wild talk! All the way west, when has Old Monkey ever behaved so disgracefully? It is a filthy creature like you—one who prizes lust above life and forgets honor at the sight of gain—who cannot tell good from bad and would be tricked into becoming someone's son-in-law, only to end up tied to a tree.” Tripitaka said, “Very well, very well. Bajie, your elder brother is seldom wrong in what he sees. Since he says so, leave her alone and let us go.” Pilgrim was overjoyed and said, “Excellent! Master will live after all. Please mount your horse. Beyond the pine forest there are households where I can beg food for you.” The four of them duly continued on their way, leaving the creature behind.

p.src: The creature, still bound to the tree, ground her teeth in hatred and said, “For years I have heard people say that Sun Wukong possesses vast supernatural powers. Having seen him today, I know the reports were indeed true. That Tang Monk has cultivated the Way in virgin purity, without losing a drop of his primal yang. I meant to seize him and mate with him so that I might become a Golden Immortal of the Great Unity, but that monkey saw through my art and rescued him. Had they untied the ropes and let me down, I could have seized him at once, and he would surely have been mine. But now a string of rambling chatter from him has led them away. Has all my labor not gone for nothing? Let me call to him a few more times and see what happens.” Without disturbing the ropes, the demon uttered several sweet and virtuous-sounding pleas, then sent them on a favorable gust to whimper into the Tang Monk's ears. And what do you suppose she called out? She cried, “Master! You abandon a living person to die without saving her; with such a heartless conscience, what scriptures do you hope to obtain by worshiping the Buddha?”

p.src: When Tang Sanzang heard the cries again from horseback, he reined in and called, “Wukong, go and rescue that woman.” Wukong said, “Master, we were on our way. Why have you begun thinking of her again?” Tang Sanzang said, “She is calling out again.” Wukong asked, “Bajie, did you hear it?” Bajie said, “My great ears covered them up, so I heard nothing.” Then he asked, “Wujing, did you hear it?” Wujing said, “I was walking ahead with the luggage and paid no attention, so I heard nothing either.” Wukong said, “Old Monkey heard nothing either. Master, what did she cry out? How is it that only you heard her?” Tang Sanzang said, “What she cries is reasonable. She says, ‘If you will not save a living soul, what scriptures can you gain by worshipping the Buddha with a darkened conscience?’ ‘To save one life is better than building a seven-storeyed pagoda.’ Hurry and rescue her; it would be a finer deed than seeking scriptures and worshipping the Buddha.” Wukong laughed. “Once your charitable impulses arise, Master, there is no medicine that can cure you. Think: since leaving the Eastern Land and journeying west, you have crossed range after range and met countless demons, who have often seized you and carried you into their caves. Whenever Old Monkey came to save you, I wielded my iron staff and killed them by the thousand and the myriad. Yet today you cannot bear to sacrifice the life of a single demon and insist on saving her?” Tang Sanzang said, “My disciple, the ancients said, ‘Do not refrain from a good deed because it is small, and do not commit an evil deed because it is small.’ Go back and save her.” Wukong said, “Since that is your will, Master, Old Monkey cannot shoulder the responsibility for what follows. If you mean to save her, I dare not weary you with further advice. If I argue for a while, you will only grow angry again. Save her if you please.” Tang Sanzang said, “Impudent ape, enough talk. Sit here while Bajie and I go and rescue her.”

p.src: Tang Sanzang returned to the woods, where he had Bajie untie the rope around the woman’s upper body and rake her lower body out of the earth. The demon settled her shoes, straightened her skirt, and happily followed Tang Sanzang out of the pine woods, where she saw Wukong. Wukong merely sneered without cease. Tang Sanzang scolded him. “You insolent ape! What are you laughing at?” Wukong said, “I am laughing because in good times you meet a dear friend, and when fortune deserts you, you encounter a lovely woman.” Tripitaka scolded him again. “Impudent macaque, do not talk nonsense. I have been a monk since I left my mother’s womb. Now I journey west by imperial command, devoutly worshipping the Buddha and seeking scriptures. I am no seeker of profit or rank, so how could my fortunes ever decline?” Wukong laughed. “Master, though you have been a monk from childhood, you know only how to read sutras and invoke the Buddha. You have never studied the laws of the realm. This woman is young and beautiful, while you and I are men who have left the world. If we travel with her and happen to meet villains who seize us and deliver us to the authorities, they will pay no heed to scripture seeking or Buddha worship but will first treat the affair as illicit relations. Even if cleared of that, we would still be charged with abducting a person. Your ordination certificate would be confiscated, Master, and you would be beaten within an inch of your life. Bajie would be sentenced to military exile. Wujing would be sentenced to service at a post station. Even Old Monkey would not escape cleanly. However eloquently I pleaded our case, I would still be convicted of misconduct.” Tripitaka shouted, “Stop your nonsense! Surely saving her life cannot bring us any trouble. We shall take her with us, and whatever happens, I will bear the whole responsibility.” Wukong said, “Though you say you will bear the responsibility, Master, you do not realize that instead of saving her, you are harming her.” Tripitaka said, “I rescued her from the woods and preserved her life. How could that be harming her?” Wukong said, “Had she remained bound in the woods for three or five days, ten days, or half a month, she would have starved to death, but at least her body would have gone whole into the realm of shades. Now that you have brought her out, you will ride a swift horse that travels like the wind, and we must keep pace with you. But the woman has tiny feet and can scarcely take a step. How can she possibly keep up? Once she falls behind, if wolves, tigers, or leopards find her and swallow her in a single bite, will you not have harmed her life instead?”

p.src: Tripitaka said, “Indeed! I am indebted to you for thinking of that. What are we to do?” Wukong laughed. “Lift her up and let her share your horse.” Tripitaka pondered and said, “How could I properly share a horse with her?” “Then how is she to travel?” Tripitaka said, “Let Bajie carry her on his back.” Wukong laughed. “Blockhead, your good fortune has arrived.” Bajie said, “‘No burden is light on a long road.’ What good fortune is there in making me carry someone?” Wukong said, “Your snout is so long that with her on your back, you can turn it around and whisper sweet nothings to her. Would that not be a fine advantage?” At this, Bajie beat his chest and leaped about, crying, “No, no! If Master wants to strike me a few times, I would rather endure the pain. If I carry her, my name will never be clean. Elder Brother has spent his whole life framing people. I will not carry her. It cannot be done.” Tripitaka said, “Very well, very well. I can still walk a few steps. I shall dismount and walk slowly with her, while Bajie leads the riderless horse.” Wukong laughed loudly. “Blockhead, you have found yourself a fine occupation: Master is kindly arranging for you to lead the horse.” Tripitaka said, “This ape is talking nonsense again. The ancients said, ‘Though a horse can travel a thousand miles, without a rider it cannot go by itself.’ If I walk slowly along the road, would you be so good as to abandon me? If I go slowly, you must all go slowly too. We shall all go down the mountain together with this lady bodhisattva. When we reach a convent, monastery, temple, or any inhabited place, we can leave her there. Then our rescue of her will be complete.” Wukong said, “Master speaks wisely. Let us hurry onward.”

p.src: Tripitaka gathered up his robes and walked in front. Wujing carried the luggage, Bajie led the riderless horse and guided the woman, while Wukong held his iron staff; thus the whole party advanced. Before they had gone twenty or thirty li, evening drew near, and they saw another complex of towers and halls. Tripitaka said, “Disciples, that must surely be a convent or temple. We shall lodge there tonight and set out early tomorrow.” Wukong said, “You are right, Master. Everyone, quicken your steps.” In an instant they reached the gate. Tripitaka instructed them, “Stand a little farther away while I go first to ask for lodging. If they can accommodate us, I shall have someone come and summon you.” They all stood beneath the shade of the willows, while Wukong alone held his iron staff and kept watch over the woman.

p.src: Tripitaka steeled his courage and passed through the second gate. He saw that both the bell tower and drum tower had collapsed. Only a single bronze bell remained, planted in the ground, its upper half white as snow and its lower half blue-green as indigo. It had stood there for many long years: the rain had bleached the upper part white, while vapors rising from the earth had coated the lower part with green verdigris. Tripitaka laid a hand upon the bell and called aloud, “O bell, once you hung high in a tower and roared; once your voice rang far beneath painted beams. Once you announced the dawn at cockcrow, and once at day’s end you tolled the coming dusk. Who knows where the Taoist who smelted your bronze has gone, or in what quarter the craftsman who cast you now dwells? I imagine both their lives have returned to the netherworld: they have left no trace, and you have lost your voice.”

p.src: The elder praised it loudly, unwittingly alarming someone inside the monastery. Inside was a lay brother who tended the incense. Hearing a human voice, he scrambled up, picked up a broken brick, and hurled it at the bell, which rang out with a clang. The elder was so frightened that he fell over. Struggling to his feet to flee, he tripped on a tree root and fell flat once more. Lying on the ground, the elder raised his head and cried, “O bell, just as this poor monk was lamenting over you, you suddenly rang out with a clang. It must be that no one ever comes along this road to the Western Heaven, and after all these long years you have turned into a spirit.”

p.src: The lay brother hurried forward, caught hold of him, and said, “My lord, please get up. The bell has not turned into a spirit; it rang because I struck it just now.” Tripitaka looked up, saw that the man was ugly and dark-featured, and said, “Are you not some demon or evil spirit? I am no ordinary man. I come from the Great Tang, and I have disciples under my command who can subdue dragons and tame tigers. If you run into them, you will scarcely escape with your life.” The lay brother knelt and said, “Do not be afraid, my lord. I am no demon. I am the lay brother who tends the incense in this monastery. Just now I heard your gracious words of praise and was about to come out to welcome you; but fearing it might be an evil ghost knocking at the gate, I picked up a broken brick and struck the bell to steady my nerves before daring to come out. Please rise, my lord.” Only then did the Tang monk recover his composure and say, “Abbot, you nearly frightened me to death. Lead me inside.”

p.src: When Tripitaka saw it, he did not dare enter, but called, “Lay brother, the front of this place is in a wretched state, yet the rear is so neat and orderly. Why is that?” The lay brother laughed. “My lord, these mountains abound in demons and fierce bandits. In clear weather they rob travelers along the mountain roads; when the skies turn overcast, they come to hide in the monastery. They knock down the Buddhist images to use as seats and carry off the timber for firewood. The monks of this monastery are weak and dare not argue with them. Therefore we yielded all the ruined buildings in front to those ruffians for their lodging, found a new group of donors, and built that monastery behind. Thus the pure and the foul each have their own place. Such are the ways of the Western Regions.” “So that is how it is,” said Tripitaka.

p.src: The lama monk came out through the gate and saw that Tripitaka had clear brows and fine eyes, a broad forehead and level crown, ears that hung to his shoulders, and hands reaching past his knees. He seemed an arhat descended to earth and was exceedingly handsome and elegant. He hurried forward, seized Tripitaka, and, grinning from ear to ear, fondled his hands and feet, felt his nose, and tugged his ears to show his affection. He led him into the abbot’s quarters. When they had exchanged bows, he asked, “Where have you come from, venerable master?” Tripitaka replied, “This disciple is an imperial envoy from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, journeying to the Great Thunderclap Monastery in the land of India in the West to worship the Buddha and obtain the scriptures. We happened to reach your honorable region at nightfall and have come especially to your noble monastery to ask lodging for one night. We shall depart early tomorrow. I beg you to grant us this convenience.” The monk laughed. “Shameful, shameful! We did not become monks out of any noble intention. It was only because the horoscope under which our parents bore us was ruled by the Solitary Canopy and we could not be raised at home that they gave us away to take the tonsure. But since you are a disciple of the Buddha, you must not tell such empty lies.” “I speak the honest truth,” said Tripitaka. The monk said, “How great is the distance from the Eastern Land to the Western Heaven? There are mountains along the way, caves within the mountains, and spirits inside the caves. You are alone and so delicately formed. How could you possibly be a scripture pilgrim?” Tripitaka replied, “Your Reverence has judged correctly. How could this poor monk have come this far alone? I have three disciples who clear paths whenever we meet a mountain and build bridges whenever we come to water. They protect me, their master, and thus I have reached your noble monastery.” “Where are your three distinguished disciples?” asked the monk. Tripitaka replied, “They are waiting outside the mountain gate.” The monk panicked. “Master, you do not know that tigers, wolves, demons, bandits, and monsters here all prey upon people. We dare not venture far even in daylight, and we bar the gates before evening falls. How could you leave people outside at this hour?” He called, “Disciples, hurry and invite them in!”

p.src: Two young lamas ran outside. At the sight of Pilgrim, they were so frightened that they fell over; when they saw Eight Rules, they fell over again. They scrambled up and flew back, crying, “Grandfather, what dreadful luck! Your disciples are nowhere to be seen; there are only three or four monsters standing at the gate!” “What do they look like?” Tripitaka asked. The young monks replied, “One has a mouth like the Thunder God’s, one has a snout like a pounding pestle, and one has a blue face and fangs. Beside them is a woman, who at least has a sleek head and powdered face.” Tripitaka laughed. “You do not recognize them. Those three ugly fellows are my disciples. The woman is someone whose life I saved in the pine forest.” The lama cried, “Good heavens! How could such a handsome master have found such ugly disciples?” Tripitaka said, “Ugly they may be, but every one of them is useful. Hurry and invite them in. If you delay any longer, the one with the Thunder God’s mouth may cause trouble. He is no ordinary mortal born and raised by human parents, and he will simply fight his way inside.”
